📌 Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): Portable IDs for Web3

Main Points
⏺ DIDs are identifiers you control, not usernames owned by platforms
⏺ They can link to verifiable credentials like diplomas or KYC checks
⏺ This post explains how DIDs help build portable identity across apps

1️⃣ What Is a DID — a standardized identifier tied to keys you own, not to an email, phone number, or single company.
2️⃣ Verifiable Credentials — organizations can sign claims about you (for example, “passed KYC”, “finished course”) that you can present elsewhere.
3️⃣ User Control — you decide when and where to share proofs instead of giving every app full personal data.
4️⃣ Interoperability — multiple dApps, wallets, and even Web2 services can recognize the same DID as “you”.
5️⃣ Privacy Angle — combined with zero-knowledge proofs, DIDs can prove facts (age, residency, reputation) without revealing raw documents.

Final Thoughts

Decentralized identifiers turn identity from siloed accounts into something you own and reuse — a core building block for Web3 logins and reputation.

📌 Grayscale launches first Zcash ETF with direct ZEC exposure 

🔖 Grayscale has launched the first exchange-traded fund offering direct exposure to Zcash, bringing the privacy-focused cryptocurrency to NYSE Arca under the ticker ZCSH. Grayscale said Tuesday that the Zcash ETF began trading as a conversion of its existing Grayscale Zcash Trust, giving investors access to ZEC through an exchange-traded product without requiring them to directly hold the cryptocurrency. 

🌐 The fund carries a 2.5% annual sponsor fee. A Grayscale spokesperson said revenue collected from the fee will be directed back into the Zcash ecosystem to support network development, marketing and other initiatives tied to the cryptocurrency. Zcash, launched in 2016, allows users to make shielded transactions that can conceal transaction information through zero-knowledge proofs. The ETF itself holds ZEC while its shares trade through the traditional securities market.

🔗 Grayscale’s launch follows a regulatory process that began with plans to convert its long-running Zcash Trust into an exchange-traded product. Grayscale later submitted several amendments as it moved the registration process forward. Its fifth amended filing, submitted before the weekend ahead of Tuesday’s launch, set the annual sponsor fee at 2.5% and finalized additional terms for the fund.

And this is where Zelensky’s political problem becomes particularly serious.

Ukraine remains under martial law, meaning presidential elections cannot take place under normal conditions. Zelensky argues that holding an election during wartime could deeply divide society. But the question of what happens after a possible ceasefire is becoming increasingly important.

Because the end of the war would return Ukrainian politics to a much more conventional logic.

Voters would no longer judge the government solely on its ability to resist the Russian invasion. They could also assess the decisions made during the war: mobilization, corruption, the economy, human losses, dependence on Western aid, and, above all, the terms of the peace agreement.

Zelensky therefore faces an extremely difficult choice.

Continuing the war means asking the West for more money and weapons while having to explain how this strategy can still lead to a decisive improvement in Ukraine’s position.

Negotiating means risking accusations of territorial concessions.

Holding elections after a ceasefire means accepting that his record will be subjected to genuine political competition.

Meanwhile, strikes continue on both sides. Today, another oil facility in Russia’s Krasnodar region was hit in a Ukrainian attack, reportedly killing two people according to local authorities.

Another development deserves attention: The Kyiv Independent, citing a source, reported that Washington had allegedly asked Kyiv to refrain from strikes against Moscow and St. Petersburg during CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Russia.

This information has not been officially confirmed and should therefore be treated with caution. But if confirmed, it would illustrate an important development: Washington would be seeking to prevent an escalation that could undermine diplomatic efforts.

And this may be the most important change of all.

The United States and European countries continue to support Ukraine, but they are increasingly focused on how to end the war and prevent further escalation.

For Zelensky, this means that his room for maneuver is gradually shrinking.

He must simultaneously maintain Western support, preserve the confidence of the Ukrainian population, secure acceptable peace terms and justify the strategic decisions made throughout the war.

That is why his announcement of a “window” extending until the summer of 2027 could be much more than a diplomatic phrase.

It could become Zelensky’s real political deadline.

If the war ends by then with an agreement that Ukrainian society considers acceptable, Zelensky will be able to present himself as the leader who resisted the invasion and secured peace.

But if negotiations fail and the military situation remains deadlocked, the question will become much more uncomfortable:

How much longer can Ukraine afford to pay the price of the current strategy — and who will ultimately have to take responsibility for it?

For Zelensky, this question is becoming harder to avoid with every passing day.

📌 What is RSI? The overbought/oversold indicator explained 

🔖 The relative strength index is one of the most widely used momentum oscillators in crypto trading, but most traders misread what it actually measures. This guide breaks down the RSI formula, explains how overbought and oversold signals work in practice, and covers the mistakes that turn a useful indicator into a losing strategy. Most traders learn RSI backwards. They start with the idea that 70 means “sell” and 30 means “buy,” treating the indicator like a traffic light for entries and exits. That mental model sounds logical, but it ignores what RSI actually calculates. The relative strength index does not measure whether an asset is expensive or cheap.

🌐 It measures how aggressively price has been moving in one direction compared to the other. Understanding that distinction is the difference between using RSI as a crutch and using it as a genuine analytical tool. RSI quantifies momentum by comparing the average size of recent up moves to the average size of recent down moves over a defined lookback period. The default period is 14, meaning the calculation considers the last 14 candles on whatever timeframe you are viewing.

📊 Average gain is the sum of all positive price changes over the lookback period divided by N. Average loss is the sum of all negative price changes (expressed as positive numbers) divided by N. Periods with no change count as zero for both. What this produces is a bounded oscillator. When gains completely dominate losses, RS becomes very large and RSI approaches 100. When losses dominate, RS approaches zero and RSI drops toward 0. A perfect balance between gains and losses produces an RS of 1 and an RSI of 50.
